ctx.x: Okay, real number four with Tex Stevens, and this is still August 29th, 1995. Okay, uh, yeah, uh, where were we? Were we talking about Frank Panae? We were moving along. Well in 19...

...his... Right after the soldiers started coming home, and then some soldiers were passing through, and like we said, things were not as integrated as they are now, and people wanted to... People had a few money. Some people were covered being, uh, turned loose and normal with three, four, five, six hundred dollars, which was a lot of money. Remember, Coca-Cola was 25 cents, uh, Coca-Cola was five cents a bottle. You could get a half a pint of liquor for 45 cents, along with a seven-up of Coke and a pitcher of…
He had the whole package. He had the package.

items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1996-01-10
items.q: he called me and he called Larry McKinley. And that's how we got on the staff to give life to the Jazz and Heritage Festival.

ctx.x: Anything else from his column strike you?

Well, there are many things that strike me when I start thinking about my classmate from Hawthorne High School, Randy the Whip, who was one of the first disc jockeys in the city of New Orleans. He was really a mechanic by trade. He had a mechanical mind. And he taught school at a big building on the corner of Jackson Avenue and doing Chapitula Street for many years. And then he left there and he became a disc jockey and started doing broadcasting on the radio. And he also was a good friend of Frank Pena because…
